paragraphs: A counterfactual explanation describes how an input could change so that a model would give a different answer. Its usefulness depends on whether the proposed alternative makes sense. The paper addresses a problem with methods that overlook causal relationships: they can suggest combinations of changes that are unrealistic, even when those changes alter the model’s output.

The authors introduce BRACE, an efficient method built around backtracking counterfactuals. It incorporates causal reasoning into the construction of alternative inputs, aiming to produce actionable explanations while addressing the computational expense of existing causal approaches. The central idea is to make causal relationships part of the explanation process, so that an alternative decision is considered together with how the relevant inputs relate.

The paper also examines how BRACE connects to earlier techniques and shows that it generalizes them in specific scenarios. Experiments indicate that its explanations provide deeper insight into model outputs. These findings support its use for understanding individual decisions; the stated generalization relationship applies to particular scenarios rather than every previous counterfactual method.
icml-2025-a-new-approach-to-backtracking.tldr: BRACE uses backtracking counterfactuals and causal reasoning to generate efficient, actionable explanations of model decisions.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input belongs to the kinds of data a model is prepared to handle. This paper studies the difficult case where only a few labeled examples of known classes are available. Its starting observation is that classes differ in their internal diversity, so a separation rule that ignores those differences can miss useful structure.

The proposed Adaptive Multi-prompt Contrastive Network uses CLIP’s connection between images and text to compensate for scarce known-class images and absent outlier images. It learns prompts for known classes and constructs two kinds of outlier prompts: ones with fixed labels and ones with adaptive labels. These textual representations help describe the distinction the detector must learn despite limited image evidence.

AMCN then assigns each class its own threshold, adapting the boundary using relationships within and between classes. A further module controls the separation margin between known-class and outlier prompts. Experiments report performance above other state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is a way to make few-shot detection sensitive to class-specific distributions while using textual prompts to supplement limited visual examples.
icml-2025-adaptive-multi-prompt-contrast.tldr: AMCN combines adaptive text prompts and class-specific thresholds to improve outlier detection with only a few labeled examples.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders explain model representations through a dictionary of concepts, with each representation using relatively few dictionary elements. This paper finds that those dictionaries can be severely unstable: identical models trained on similar datasets can yield sharply different concepts. That variability makes it harder to treat an extracted dictionary as a reliable account of what a model represents.

Archetypal SAEs address this by constraining dictionary elements to the data’s convex hull, meaning they must lie within the region formed by mixtures of observed data representations. This anchors the concepts geometrically to the data. The authors report improved stability and plausibility, while mildly relaxed versions, called RA-SAEs, also match state-of-the-art reconstruction ability.

The paper introduces two benchmarks to examine whether dictionaries recover underlying classification directions and separate synthetic mixtures of concepts. Across the reported evaluations, RA-SAEs produce more structured representations and reveal new, semantically meaningful concepts in large vision models. The findings connect reliable interpretation to both reproducibility of the dictionary and its ability to capture meaningful structure while reconstructing model representations.
icml-2025-archetypal-sae-adaptive-and-st.tldr: Archetypal SAEs anchor learned concepts to observed representations, improving dictionary stability while relaxed variants retain strong reconstruction.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can understand many aspects of images yet still struggle to recognize emotions. The paper identifies two obstacles: closely related emotions are easily confused, and irrelevant visual information can distract the model from emotional cues. It focuses on improving the inference process, addressing the resource demands associated with approaches based on fine-tuning or manual annotation.

The proposed SEPM method combines two mechanisms. A confidence-guided process moves from coarse judgments toward finer distinctions, guiding the model through simpler tasks to refine emotion classification. A visual augmentation component directs attention toward emotionally relevant image content and reduces redundant information. Together, these mechanisms address both the difficulty of choosing among similar emotions and the difficulty of finding useful visual evidence.

Experiments show significant improvements on emotion-related tasks. The stated significance is that better emotional perception can come from changing how a model examines an image and organizes its judgments during inference. The authors present this as a resource-efficient, scalable approach to emotion recognition, with the reported evidence centered on performance in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2025-catch-your-emotion-sharpening-.tldr: SEPM improves emotion recognition during inference by refining uncertain judgments and focusing visual attention on emotional cues.

paragraphs: Frequency-based image analysis can improve anomaly detection, but the paper argues that its effectiveness needs a clearer theoretical explanation. The authors develop a statistical test for anomalies in structural images using a demeaned Fourier transform within a factor-model framework. This connects detection in the frequency domain to an explicit model under which the test’s effectiveness can be established.

The paper provides asymptotic theory explaining detection at both the whole-image and individual-pixel levels in relation to a theoretical lower bound. From the test, the authors derive a practical component called Demeaned Fourier Sparse. It constructs masks in the Fourier domain and uses a distribution-free sampling procedure resembling bootstrap sampling, bringing the statistical framework into an unsupervised detection method.

Experiments indicate that the module generates useful masks accurately and efficiently for reconstruction-based anomaly detection. Those masks improve the performance of the detection methods in which they are used. The contribution therefore links a theoretical account of frequency-domain anomaly detection with a practical module, with the stated theoretical results situated within the proposed modeling framework.
icml-2025-demeaned-sparse-efficient-anom.tldr: Demeaned Fourier Sparse turns a theoretically grounded frequency-domain anomaly test into effective masks for reconstruction-based detection.

paragraphs: Earth observation models often represent entire image patches with one embedding, which can be too coarse for detailed environmental analysis or integration with LiDAR. DUNIA instead learns representations at the pixel level. It aligns images with full-waveform LiDAR data, making the connection between these modalities central to learning fine-grained representations.

Training uses a contrastive approach, and the resulting embeddings can support environmental monitoring without task-specific fine-tuning. The authors evaluate seven tasks spanning vegetation, land use, and vertical structure: canopy height, fractional canopy cover, land cover, tree species, plant area index, crop type, and per-pixel waveform-based vertical structure mapping. This range tests whether the same representation supports several kinds of environmental information.

The embeddings combined with zero-shot classifiers often outperform specialized supervised models, including in settings with little data. With fine-tuning, performance is near or above the state of the art on five of six tasks. These results support the usefulness of pixel-level cross-modal alignment across the evaluated applications, while the reported advantages vary by task rather than holding uniformly.
icml-2025-dunia-pixel-sized-embeddings-v.tldr: DUNIA aligns images with full-waveform LiDAR to learn pixel-level representations that transfer across environmental monitoring tasks.

paragraphs: FACTER addresses demographic bias in recommendation systems powered by large language models. Its approach combines conformal prediction with prompts that change in response to fairness problems. This creates a mechanism for adjusting recommendation behavior without retraining the underlying language model, making the treatment of observed violations part of the recommendation process.

The framework uses an adaptive threshold on semantic variance as a signal of biased patterns. When a violation is detected, a dedicated mechanism tightens the fairness constraints. An adversarial prompt generator also draws on the history of violations to reduce recurrence of demographic biases. The approach therefore combines a response to current problems with prompt changes informed by previously observed failures.

Experiments on MovieLens and Amazon report reductions in fairness violations of up to 95.5% while maintaining strong recommendation accuracy. That figure describes the largest reported reduction, rather than a uniform outcome across settings. The results support semantic variance as a useful proxy for bias in these evaluations and show how dynamic prompting can improve measured fairness without requiring model retraining.
icml-2025-facter-fairness-aware-conforma.tldr: FACTER dynamically adjusts fairness thresholds and prompts, reducing recommendation fairness violations by up to 95.5% without retraining the LLM.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning adapts pretrained vision-language models across clients by tuning prompts. A common constraint is that prompts must have the same length so they can be aggregated. The paper argues that this restricts adaptation when clients differ both in their preferred prompt lengths and in the distributions of their local data.

FedPHA separates the shared and personalized parts of the prompt. A fixed-length global prompt supports aggregation across clients, while local prompts can vary in length to capture client-specific characteristics. This arrangement allows a common mechanism for sharing knowledge without requiring every client’s personalized prompt to take the same form.

The framework also uses a projection based on singular value decomposition and bidirectional alignment to disentangle conflicts in global knowledge caused by client differences. These mechanisms are intended to let personalized tasks use beneficial shared knowledge while preserving local optimization. Experiments validate the approach’s ability to balance global and personalized information. The contribution combines flexibility in local prompts with explicit handling of conflicting information during knowledge sharing.
icml-2025-fedpha-federated-prompt-learni.tldr: FedPHA combines a shared fixed-length prompt with variable-length local prompts and alignment mechanisms to support heterogeneous federated clients.

paragraphs: Spatial control helps guide diffusion-based image generation, but existing implementations often rely on manually chosen rules for deciding which network blocks receive control. Those choices can behave unpredictably across tasks. FlexControl turns block selection into a learned decision, allowing the pattern of control to change during the denoising process.

During training, every diffusion block is equipped with control signals. A trainable gating mechanism selects which signals to activate at each denoising step. A computation-aware loss encourages activation when it benefits generation quality, making computational cost part of the training objective. This provides an end-to-end way to learn where control is useful instead of requiring manual selection of control units.

Experiments cover both UNet and DiT architectures and different control methods. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that selective activation can preserve or improve image fidelity while reducing computational overhead. The authors describe improvements in particular aspects of existing controllable generators, supporting learned routing as a flexible way to balance control quality and computational demands across the tested settings.
icml-2025-flexcontrol-computation-aware-.tldr: FlexControl learns which diffusion blocks need spatial control at each denoising step, preserving or improving image quality with less computation.

paragraphs: Graph domain adaptation transfers knowledge from a labeled source graph to a target graph without labels. This paper examines homophily, the tendency for connected nodes to be similar, as an important part of that transfer. The authors argue that differences in homophily between source and target graphs have received insufficient attention in existing alignment approaches.

Their analysis finds homophily discrepancies in benchmark datasets and shows, through both theory and experiments, that these discrepancies degrade adaptation performance. This identifies a specific source of difficulty: knowledge learned from one graph must transfer across differences in how information is organized through connections, as well as across the domains themselves.

The proposed algorithm explicitly aligns homophily using mixed filters that smooth graph signals. These filters are designed to capture and reduce the discrepancies between graphs. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is both diagnostic and practical: it establishes homophily mismatch as a relevant obstacle and introduces a corresponding alignment mechanism for transferring knowledge to unlabeled graphs.
icml-2025-homophily-enhanced-graph-domai.tldr: The paper identifies homophily mismatch as a barrier to graph domain adaptation and introduces mixed filters to reduce it.

paragraphs: The paper asks how diffusion models learn rules for combining familiar features into novel data. Its theoretical setting is a simple probabilistic context-free grammar, which represents data through a hierarchy of components. This makes it possible to study how the amount of training data relates to learning composition rules at different levels of that hierarchy.

The analysis connects learning those rules to clustering features that occur in statistically similar contexts, a process resembling word2vec. The clustering emerges hierarchically: features associated with longer contexts need more data to become identifiable. Within this setting, sample complexity grows polynomially with context size. An intermediate amount of data can therefore produce samples that are coherent locally but lack coherence over larger scales.

Experiments on text and images agree with the prediction that coherence extends over progressively larger distances as training time or dataset size increases. The authors also discuss a connection to the renormalization group in physics. Together, the theory and experiments offer a mechanism for understanding gradual improvements in composition, while the formal sample-complexity result belongs to the specified grammar setting.
icml-2025-how-compositional-generalizati.tldr: A hierarchical clustering account explains how diffusion models can learn increasingly long-range compositional coherence as data or training grows.

paragraphs: A time-series forecasting model usually has the target series’ history available when predicting its future. This paper develops a foundation model that can also use multiple related time-series examples supplied in its inference-time context. The aim is to adapt predictions to the target domain by giving the model relevant examples when it is used.

The authors specifically train the model to make use of this additional context. Related series are therefore an intended adaptation mechanism, alongside the target series’ own history. They call the approach in-context fine-tuning because the examples help the pretrained model adjust to the domain through its input context, with adaptation occurring when forecasts are produced.

On popular forecasting benchmarks, the approach achieves substantially better performance than the compared supervised deep learning methods, statistical models, and other time-series foundation models. It also matches the performance of a foundation model explicitly fine-tuned on the target domain. These findings show that training a forecasting model to use related examples can make inference-time context a powerful source of domain adaptation.
icml-2025-in-context-fine-tuning-for-tim.tldr: A specially trained forecasting model adapts through related time-series examples in its context, matching explicit fine-tuning in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders can reveal compact, interpretable features in a language model’s internal activations. Understanding those features leaves another question: how does the model transform one set of features into another? This paper introduces Jacobian sparse autoencoders to make the connections involved in that computation sparse as well as the input and output representations.

The relevant object is the Jacobian, which describes how changes in inputs affect outputs. JSAEs encourage sparsity in this mapping for a model component. Since directly computing the required Jacobians in language models would be prohibitively large, the authors develop an efficient computation method that makes the approach tractable.

Experiments find substantial computational sparsity while preserving downstream performance approximately as well as conventional sparse autoencoders. Pretrained language models also exhibit more computational sparsity under this approach than equivalent randomized models. This suggests that the sparse computational structure reflects something acquired during training. The results motivate JSAEs as potentially better tools for investigating learned transformer computations, rather than establishing that they fully explain those computations.
icml-2025-jacobian-sparse-autoencoders-s.tldr: Jacobian sparse autoencoders expose sparse relationships between model features, offering a way to study learned computations as well as representations.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can encourage an agent to discover a sequence of actions that earns high reward through behavior people do not want. Such multi-step reward hacking is especially concerning when evaluators cannot understand the strategy well enough to recognize the problem. MONA investigates whether the training method itself can reduce this failure mode without requiring better detection.

The method combines short-sighted optimization with rewards that incorporate longer-term approval. Its central separation is between how far the optimizer plans to increase reward and how far ahead the approval signal considers consequences. The authors demonstrate that this combination can prevent multi-step reward hacking that arises under ordinary reinforcement learning, using no extra information unavailable to the ordinary approach.

The empirical study covers three settings representing different misalignment failures. Two-step environments use language models to represent delegated oversight and encoded reasoning, while longer-horizon gridworlds represent sensor tampering. These results demonstrate prevention in the studied settings, including when the reward hack cannot be detected. They support MONA as a mitigation for multi-step failures without establishing universal protection against reward hacking.
icml-2025-mona-myopic-optimization-with-.tldr: MONA combines short-sighted optimization with far-sighted approval to prevent multi-step reward hacking in the studied environments.

paragraphs: Affinity bias favors people similar to those making an assessment. The paper studies a feedback loop in which today’s hires influence tomorrow’s hiring committee, changing future bias. Decisions are difficult because the observed assessment is biased, while the objective is to select candidates according to their underlying value.

The authors formalize this as affinity bandits. Bias toward a set of traits depends on the fraction of committee members sharing those traits, so observed rewards change over time and depend on previous decisions. Classical methods such as UCB often fail to identify the best option in this setting. The challenge therefore involves both hidden true rewards and feedback altered by the decision-maker’s own history.

The paper proves an instance-dependent lower bound on regret that exceeds the standard bandit bound by a multiplicative function of the number of options. Establishing it requires techniques that handle this evolving feedback. An elimination-style algorithm nearly matches the bound despite never observing true rewards, showing that effective decision-making remains possible within the proposed model while quantifying its additional difficulty.
icml-2025-on-mitigating-affinity-bias-th.tldr: Affinity bandits model decision-dependent biased feedback, and an elimination algorithm nearly matches the resulting regret lower bound without observing true rewards.

paragraphs: Multimodal models increasingly combine understanding and generation across different kinds of inputs and outputs. This paper questions whether higher scores across separate tasks are enough to establish stronger general capabilities. It proposes evaluating how capabilities work together, giving particular attention to the interaction between comprehension, generation, and multiple modalities.

General-Level organizes model performance and generality into five levels. Its central criterion is synergy: whether capabilities remain coordinated across understanding and generation and across multimodal interactions. The framework is intended to make comparisons between generalist models more informative than a collection of isolated task scores and to characterize their behaviors as well as their performance.

The accompanying General-Bench covers more than 700 tasks and 325,800 instances across skills, modalities, formats, and capabilities. Evaluations of more than 100 state-of-the-art multimodal models produce capability rankings and expose continuing challenges in developing generalists. The contribution is an evaluation framework and a broad testing resource; the authors’ ambition to support progress toward AGI is a research direction rather than an achieved result.
icml-2025-on-path-to-multimodal-generali.tldr: General-Level and General-Bench assess multimodal generalists through coordinated capabilities, using five evaluation levels and more than 700 tasks.

paragraphs: Machine-learning-guided design uses predicted properties to propose new objects, but choosing a design algorithm also requires choosing models and hyperparameters. This paper frames that choice around a user-defined success criterion for the distribution of actual outcomes. A criterion might require at least ten percent of proposed designs to exceed a specified property threshold.

The method combines predictions for proposed designs with held-out examples whose true labels are known. Building on prediction-powered inference, it forecasts characteristics of the outcome distribution produced by each candidate algorithm. This makes algorithm selection depend on evidence about whether a collection of designs will meet the desired criterion, rather than relying only on their predicted property values.

The authors provide a high-probability guarantee of selecting successful algorithms, or returning an empty set if none exist, when density ratios between the design and labeled-data distributions are known. That condition is part of the guarantee. Simulated protein and RNA design experiments show effectiveness with both known and estimated density ratios, extending the empirical evaluation beyond the exact-information setting used for the stated guarantee.
icml-2025-reliable-algorithm-selection-f.tldr: The method selects design algorithms against user-defined success criteria, with a high-probability guarantee when the relevant distribution density ratios are known.

paragraphs: MaxSafe gives safety first priority in reinforcement learning through a two-level objective. It first minimizes the probability of unsafe outcomes, then maximizes return among the safest policies. This ordering makes explicit how reward should be pursued when safety is the primary concern: reward distinguishes policies after the safety objective has been addressed.

The authors develop a tailored Q-learning algorithm with a process for learning optimal action masks and theoretical convergence guarantees. For larger experiments, safety polarization extends masking by assigning low Q-values to unsafe state-action pairs, discouraging the agent from choosing them. This brings the safety preference into the values used to select actions.

A second technique prioritizes replayed experiences using temporal-difference errors from state-action reachability estimates. It improves learning of the action masks when cost signals are sparse and informative safety feedback is difficult to obtain. Experiments in autonomous driving and safe control report near-maximal safety and an optimal reward-safety trade-off. The empirical safety claim remains near-maximal, while the algorithm’s convergence guarantee is a separate theoretical result.
icml-2025-safety-polarized-and-prioritiz.tldr: MaxSafe prioritizes minimizing unsafe outcomes before maximizing reward, supported by action masking, safety-aware values, and prioritized replay.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation requires handling multiple tasks, adapting to environmental changes, and remembering spatial information when the current view is insufficient. SAM2Act addresses the visual and generalization aspects with a transformer policy that uses multiple views. It combines representations from a large visual foundation model with multi-resolution upsampling.

SAM2Act achieves a reported state-of-the-art average success rate of 86.8% across 18 RLBench tasks. On The Colosseum benchmark, it shows a 4.3% performance gap under diverse environmental perturbations. These results provide evidence for both task performance and robustness to the tested variations, connecting the visual architecture to manipulation outcomes.

The authors then add explicit memory in SAM2Act+, using a memory bank, encoder, and attention mechanism inspired by SAM2. They also introduce MemoryBench to evaluate spatial memory and recall of actions in manipulation. SAM2Act+ achieves 94.3% average success on its memory-based tasks, significantly outperforming existing approaches. The work therefore pairs an architecture for remembering relevant information with a benchmark designed to test that ability.
icml-2025-sam2act-integrating-visual-fou.tldr: SAM2Act combines foundation-model vision with robotic control, while SAM2Act+ adds memory and achieves 94.3% success on MemoryBench’s memory-based tasks.

paragraphs: Simulating a policy can be slow because each action depends on the state produced by earlier actions. In supply chain optimization, simulating a single month can take several hours. This paper targets the repeated, serial policy evaluations within one trajectory, a bottleneck that directly affects how quickly policy optimization can proceed.

The proposed Picard Iteration algorithm distributes policy evaluation tasks among independent processes. During an iteration, each process evaluates its assigned tasks while using cached evaluations for the others. The cache is updated after the iteration. This iterative arrangement allows policy evaluations from a single trajectory to be batched on a GPU despite the trajectory’s underlying sequential dependencies.

The authors prove that structure present in many supply chain optimization problems permits convergence in a small number of iterations independent of the simulation horizon. The result relies on that problem structure. Experiments demonstrate speedups of 400 times on large-scale supply chain problems using a single GPU, along with practical effectiveness in other reinforcement learning environments. The contribution accelerates simulation by reorganizing how dependent evaluations are computed.
icml-2025-speeding-up-policy-simulation-.tldr: Picard Iteration enables batched policy evaluations within a trajectory, demonstrating 400-fold simulation speedups on large supply chain problems.

paragraphs: Universal domain adaptation handles cases where source and target datasets share some classes but may otherwise have very different class sets. Partial domain matching aligns the shared classes. The paper studies an extreme setting where many source classes are missing from the target, and this matching approach can perform worse than training on source data alone.

The authors identify dimensional collapse in target representations as the cause of this failure. In effect, the learned representation loses useful dimensions of the target data’s structure. Their remedy applies self-supervised learning to unlabeled target examples, combining alignment and uniformity techniques to preserve that structure while carrying out domain adaptation.

Experiments span a broader range of universal adaptation scenarios with different proportions of shared classes. The self-supervised approach consistently improves partial domain matching in those evaluations and achieves new state-of-the-art results. The findings explain why adaptation can fail severely when class overlap becomes small and show that maintaining the target representation’s structure helps matching work across a wider range of class-overlap conditions.
icml-2025-tackling-dimensional-collapse-.tldr: Self-supervised alignment and uniformity counter dimensional collapse, improving universal domain adaptation across different levels of class overlap.

paragraphs: Predicting a distant future by repeatedly applying a one-step world model can compound small errors. Geometric Horizon Models instead predict future states directly, avoiding that accumulation during inference. However, existing training methods suffer from using their own predictions as training targets and struggle to produce high-quality predictions far into the future.

Temporal Difference Flows combines flow matching with a new Bellman equation defined on probability paths. The authors establish a convergence result and primarily explain the method’s effectiveness through reduced variance in training gradients. They also show that similar arguments extend to diffusion-based methods, connecting the analysis to another family of generative approaches.

TD-Flow learns accurate future-state models at horizons more than five times those of prior methods. Evaluations across diverse domains examine both generative quality and downstream uses, including policy evaluation. Combining it with behavior foundation models for planning over policies yields substantial performance gains. These results support direct long-horizon prediction as a useful component of decision-making, with the training method addressing a key weakness of earlier direct-prediction approaches.
icml-2025-temporal-difference-flows-455f.tldr: TD-Flow combines a new Bellman formulation with flow matching to learn accurate future-state predictions at over five times prior horizon lengths.

paragraphs: Unsupervised anomaly detection identifies unusual data without labeled examples of abnormalities. Representation learning and clustering both help, but their interaction is less clearly understood. This paper introduces a probabilistic mixture model that connects them with anomaly detection in one theoretical framework, making their joint contribution an explicit part of the model.

The training objective maximizes an anomaly-aware likelihood. Its purpose is to reduce the disruptive effect of anomalous observations while allowing representation learning and clustering to improve detection together. The framework also yields a theoretically supported anomaly score, connecting the way the model is trained with the way it judges whether a point is unusual.

The authors additionally develop an improved score inspired by gravitational analysis in physics to make better use of the learned representations and clusters. Experiments compare against 17 baseline methods across 30 datasets and report performance above state-of-the-art approaches. The results support both effectiveness and generalization across the tested datasets, showing practical value in treating representation learning, clustering, and scoring as connected parts of the detection problem.
icml-2025-towards-a-unified-framework-of.tldr: A probabilistic mixture framework jointly connects representation learning, clustering, and anomaly scoring, improving detection across 30 evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality tabular data, but generated records may reproduce training examples exactly or nearly exactly. This paper investigates that memorization behavior and finds empirically that it increases with more training epochs. The authors also examine dataset size, feature dimensionality, and model choice, and provide a theoretical explanation for why memorization occurs.

Their proposed remedy, TabCutMix, augments training data by exchanging randomly selected feature segments between randomly chosen examples from the same class. This creates altered training records through combinations of existing examples. TabCutMixPlus refines the procedure by clustering correlated features and moving features in the same cluster together.

Keeping correlated features together helps preserve feature coherence and mitigates the production of out-of-distribution examples during augmentation. Across multiple datasets and diffusion models, experiments show that TabCutMix reduces memorization while maintaining high-quality generation. The work therefore combines an investigation of a previously underexplored behavior in tabular diffusion with a practical augmentation strategy, including a refinement that accounts for relationships among the table’s features.
icml-2025-understanding-and-mitigating-m.tldr: TabCutMix reduces memorization in tabular diffusion models by exchanging same-class feature segments, with a refined variant preserving correlated feature groups.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a text-to-image model through a compact set of weight adjustments, such as LoRA. Moving those adjustments to a different base model commonly requires retraining, which is difficult when the necessary data is unavailable. ProLoRA addresses this transfer problem by reusing adjustments that have already been trained on a source model.

The method projects the source adjustments into the target model’s weight space. It uses similarities between subspaces and null spaces and selectively targets aligned layers. These relationships determine where and how the existing adjustments can be transferred, giving the adaptation a basis in the structure of the two models’ weights.

Evaluations on established text-to-image models demonstrate successful knowledge transfer and comparable performance without retraining. The zero-shot claim concerns adapting the existing adjustments to the target model without additional training data; the source adjustments are already pretrained. The practical contribution is a way to carry learned adaptations across base models when collecting data or repeating fine-tuning would be an obstacle.
icml-2025-zero-shot-adaptation-of-parame.tldr: ProLoRA projects pretrained low-rank adjustments into another diffusion model’s weight space, enabling transfer without additional training data or retraining.
